shortExplanation: The pair in choice C has product $-36$; all four other pairs have product $36$.
detailedSteps: The positive times negative product is $(1/2)(-72)=-36$.
commonMistakes: Two negative factors have positive product, while exactly one negative factor gives a negative product.
difficultyNotes: Check the sign before multiplying magnitudes.

shortExplanation: Dividing numerator and denominator by $7$ gives $7/12$, whose entries sum to $19$.
detailedSteps: The greatest common divisor of $49$ and $84$ is $7$.
The fraction becomes $7/12$, and $7+12=19$.
commonMistakes: The sum must be taken after reduction.
difficultyNotes: A reduced fraction determines the requested numerator and denominator.

shortExplanation: The number $51$ has prime factor $17$, larger than every prime factor of the other choices.
detailedSteps: The factorizations are $39=3\cdot13$, $51=3\cdot17$, $77=7\cdot11$, $91=7\cdot13$, and $121=11^2$.
The largest prime factors are respectively $13,17,11,13,11$, so choose $51$.
commonMistakes: The largest number need not have the largest prime factor.
difficultyNotes: Compare factors, not the original numbers.

shortExplanation: The factors $1000$, $0.1993$, and $10$ multiply to $1993$, leaving another factor $1993$.
detailedSteps: Combine the powers of ten: $1000\cdot10\cdot0.1993=10000\cdot0.1993=1993$.
The whole expression is therefore $1993\cdot1993=1993^2$.
commonMistakes: Move the decimal four places because the combined multiplier is $10000$.
difficultyNotes: Regroup the powers of ten before multiplying.

shortExplanation: The two patterned groups each occupy one quarter of the circle, while the unshaded group occupies one half.
detailedSteps: The bar heights must have ratio $1:1:2$ in the order dotted, hatched, unshaded.
Graph C has equal first two bars and a third bar twice as tall, matching the circle graph.
commonMistakes: Equal-looking patterns do not determine frequency; the areas of their sectors do.
difficultyNotes: Relative bar heights encode the same proportions as sector areas.

shortExplanation: Feeding the children uses three cans, and the remaining two cans feed six adults.
detailedSteps: The children require $15/5=3$ cans.
There are $5-3=2$ cans left, each feeding three adults, so the answer is $2(3)=6$.
commonMistakes: Adults and children use different amounts per person.
difficultyNotes: Convert the children count into cans before counting adults.

shortExplanation: Three copies of $3^3$ equal $3\cdot3^3=3^4$.
detailedSteps: Factor out the common term: $3^3+3^3+3^3=3(3^3)$.
Multiplying powers with the same base adds their exponents: $3^1\cdot3^3=3^4$.
commonMistakes: Exponents add when powers multiply, not when three terms are directly added.
difficultyNotes: Factorization turns a repeated sum into a product.

shortExplanation: Sixty pills provide $120$ half-pill doses, covering about $240$ days, or eight months.
detailedSteps: The number of doses is $60/(1/2)=120$.
One dose is taken every two days, so the supply covers approximately $120(2)=240$ days.
Using about thirty days per month gives eight months.
commonMistakes: The dose is half a pill every two days, not half a pill every day.
difficultyNotes: There are two different factors of two in the dose schedule.

shortExplanation: The inner table lookups both give $3$, and the final lookup gives $3*3=4$.
detailedSteps: Read row $2$, column $4$ to obtain $2*4=3$.
Read row $1$, column $3$ to obtain $1*3=3$.
Finally read row $3$, column $3$ to obtain $4$.
commonMistakes: The star is defined by the table and is not ordinary multiplication.
difficultyNotes: Every operation must be looked up in the supplied table.

shortExplanation: March has a drop of $2.50$ dollars, larger than the other monthly decreases.
detailedSteps: The graph gives drops of $0.50$ dollars in January, $2.50$ in March, $1.50$ in May, and $2.00$ in June.
February and April show increases. Comparing the four drops identifies March.
commonMistakes: The lowest price and the largest drop need not occur in the same month.
difficultyNotes: Use each labeled time interval rather than its endpoint price.

shortExplanation: The median is the forty-first score, and it lies in the interval labeled $70$.
detailedSteps: For $81$ scores, the middle rank is $(81+1)/2=41$.
The frequencies through the interval labeled $65$ total $1+2+4+5+6+10=28$.
The next interval, labeled $70$, has $14$ scores and contains ranks $29$ through $42$, including rank $41$.
commonMistakes: The highest bar identifies the modal interval, not necessarily the median interval.
difficultyNotes: Cumulative frequencies locate the middle rank.

shortExplanation: Placing minus, plus, then multiplication gives $5-4+6\cdot3=19$.
detailedSteps: The assignment uses each required operation once: $5-4+6\cdot3$.
Multiply first to obtain $5-4+18=19$.
The other five assignments give $23,17,26,-16,-9$, none of which is another listed answer.
commonMistakes: Standard multiplication precedence still applies after the signs are inserted.
difficultyNotes: There are only six possible operation assignments.

shortExplanation: The four letters have total area $39$, leaving $75-39=36$ unshaded square units.
detailedSteps: The full sign has area $5\cdot15=75$. Count the letter areas by unit-width strokes.
The H contains two five-unit stems and a one-unit crosspiece, area $11$. The E has a five-unit stem plus three two-unit extensions, also $11$. The L has area $5+2=7$.
The P has a five-unit stem, two two-unit horizontal extensions, and one connecting unit on the right, area $10$. Thus the unshaded area is $75-(11+11+7+10)=36$.
commonMistakes: Count overlap at joined strokes only once.
difficultyNotes: Unit-width strokes provide a direct area count.

detailedSteps: The entry in row two, column one cannot be $1$ because that column already has $1$, and cannot be $2$ because that row already has $2$. It is therefore $3$.
The rest of row two gives $A=1$. Column one then ends with $2$.
Row one must have $3$ in its middle position because column two already contains $2$. Its last entry is $2$, forcing $B=3$ in the last column.
commonMistakes: Use both row and column exclusions when placing each number.
difficultyNotes: The two given diagonal entries force the rest of the table.

shortExplanation: The remaining total is $4(85)-97=243$, whose mean is $81$.
detailedSteps: The four numbers sum to $4(85)=340$.
After removing $97$, the other three sum to $243$, so their average is $243/3=81$.
keyIdeas: Removing one value from a mean
commonMistakes: Subtract the removed value from the total, not directly from the mean.
difficultyNotes: Totals make a changing mean manageable.

shortExplanation: Evaluating from the innermost sum gives $2+1/3=7/3$, then $1+3/7=10/7$, whose reciprocal is $7/10$.
detailedSteps: The inner denominator is $2+1/3=7/3$. Its reciprocal is $3/7$.
The outer denominator is $1+3/7=10/7$.
Taking the final reciprocal gives $7/10$.
commonMistakes: Work from the deepest fraction outward; each horizontal bar changes the grouping.
difficultyNotes: Nested fractions are evaluated from the inside outward.

shortExplanation: The interior surface is the remaining sheet after four $25$-unit corners are removed: $600-100=500$.
detailedSteps: The starting rectangle has area $20\cdot30=600$.
Each removed corner has area $5^2=25$, and there are four corners.
Folding changes the shape but preserves the area of the remaining material: $600-4(25)=500$.
commonMistakes: The requested quantity is surface area, not the box volume.
alternativeMethods: The base is $10\times20$, and the four walls have total area $2(5\cdot10)+2(5\cdot20)=300$. Their sum is $200+300=500$.
difficultyNotes: Folding does not change the area of the material.

shortExplanation: The rectangle has area $640$; each excluded triangle has area $160$, leaving $320$.
detailedSteps: The rectangle has area $32\cdot20=640$. Since $B$ is the midpoint of $AC$, $BC=16$, so triangle $BCD$ has area $16(20)/2=160$.
Since $F$ is the midpoint of $AE$, $EF=10$, so triangle $DEF$ has area $32(10)/2=160$.
The quadrilateral occupies the rest: $640-160-160=320$.
commonMistakes: The slanted segments need not be measured to compute the two right-triangle areas.
difficultyNotes: Midpoints halve the legs of the excluded triangles.

shortExplanation: Each corresponding pair differs by $1800$, and there are $93$ pairs.
detailedSteps: Pair $1901$ with $101$, $1902$ with $102$, and so on through $1993$ with $193$. Every difference is $1800$.
The inclusive number of terms is $1993-1901+1=93$.
commonMistakes: Inclusive counting requires adding one to the difference of the endpoints.
difficultyNotes: Pairing corresponding terms avoids two large sums.

shortExplanation: The number has $91$ nines followed by $07$, so its digit sum is $91(9)+7=826$.
detailedSteps: The first term has $91$ nines followed by two zeroes; adding seven changes only its final digit.
The resulting digit sum is $91\cdot9+0+7=826$.
commonMistakes: Count the trailing two positions separately from the string of nines.
difficultyNotes: The borrow structure determines the full digit string.

shortExplanation: The new area is $1.2\cdot1.5=1.8$ times the old area, an increase of $80\%$.
detailedSteps: Let the original area be $LW$. The new area is $(1.2L)(1.5W)=1.8LW$.
The increase is $0.8LW$, or $80\%$ of the original.
commonMistakes: Adding the two percentage increases omits their combined effect.
difficultyNotes: The new area factor is a product of length factors.

shortExplanation: Pages through $99$ use twenty twos, and pages $102$ and $112$ use the last two; the next needed two is on page $120$.
detailedSteps: From $1$ to $99$, the units digit is $2$ ten times and the tens digit is $2$ ten times. Page $22$ correctly contributes twice, giving twenty twos.
From $100$ through $119$, only $102$ and $112$ contain the digit $2$, so the supply of twenty-two is exactly exhausted.
Every page through $119$ can be labeled, but $120$ requires another two.
keyIdeas: Counting repeated digits in page labels
commonMistakes: Count occurrences, not merely pages containing the digit.
difficultyNotes: A digit repeated on one page consumes two copies.

shortExplanation: P is necessarily first, while S follows P, T, and Q; neither can be third.
detailedSteps: The conditions force the chain $P<T<Q<S$, and also $P<R$. Therefore P precedes every runner, and S has at least three runners before it.
The orders $P,R,T,Q,S$, $P,T,Q,R,S$, and $P,T,R,Q,S$ show that T, Q, and R, respectively, can finish third.
Exactly P and S cannot take third place.
commonMistakes: Prove that each remaining runner can actually occupy third, rather than relying only on exclusions.
difficultyNotes: Exclusions and explicit witness orders together establish the answer.

shortExplanation: Row twelve ends at $144$; the entry above $142$ is one position before the preceding row end, $121$, hence $120$.
detailedSteps: Row $n$ has $2n-1$ entries and ends with $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2$.
Since $121<142\le144$, the number $142$ is in row twelve, two places left of its last entry $144$.
The rows are centered, so the previous row ends one column left of $144$, directly above $143$. Its final entry is $121$, and the entry directly above $142$ is therefore $120$.
commonMistakes: The shorter row is centered; its right edge does not align with the right edge of the next row.
difficultyNotes: Both row endpoints and centered alignment matter.

shortExplanation: A $45^\circ$ rotation centered at a grid intersection covers twelve cells, placing the maximum in the category “12 or more.”
detailedSteps: Put the card center at a grid vertex and rotate it by $45^\circ$. Its four tips are $a=1.5/\sqrt2$ units from its center along the grid axes; $1<a<2$.

The card covers positive area in all four cells meeting at the center. Each of its four tips extends past a grid line one unit away and covers positive area in the two cells on opposite sides of that axis, adding eight distinct cells.
This construction covers $4+8=12$ cells, so the maximum is at least twelve and the correct option is E. An exact global maximum is not needed to choose among the stated ranges.
commonMistakes: Keeping the card parallel to the grid misses the useful rotated configurations. Touching at a point alone would not count as covering positive area.
difficultyNotes: A lower-bound construction suffices for the offered final range.
